exam: What is the first step in managing a 2‑year‑old with a seizure and fever? — Check temperature, give antipyretic, and observe; if seizure >1 min, give diazepam.
How would you differentiate a simple febrile seizure from meningitis? — Look for neck stiffness, photophobia, and altered consciousness; consider LP if present.
Why is phenobarbital avoided in acute febrile seizures? — It has sedative effects and is unnecessary; benzodiazepines are preferred.
What is the significance of a normal CBC in a child with a febrile seizure? — It does not rule out bacterial infection; clinical assessment remains paramount.
When is a lumbar puncture indicated in a febrile child with seizures? — If focal signs, altered sensorium, or persistent fever >48 h.
Why should antiepileptics not be started after a single febrile seizure? — They are not indicated; they carry side‑effects and do not reduce recurrence.
What red flag would prompt immediate transfer to a higher‑level facility? — Seizure >15 min, focal deficit, or signs of meningitis.
How does malaria contribute to febrile seizures in endemic areas? — Parasite‑induced fever and cerebral involvement can trigger seizures.
ai.title: Febrile Convulsions
ai.subject: Paediatrics
ai.summary: Febrile convulsions are brief seizures in children 6–60 months triggered by fever. They are benign, self‑limited, and usually do not indicate epilepsy. Prompt assessment rules out serious infection or metabolic disturbance.

sections.p: A seizure lasting <15 min, occurring in a child 6–60 months with a temperature >38 °C, and no prior afebrile seizures. Diagnosis is clinical; EEG is not required unless atypical features appear.
Seizures are classified as simple (tonic–clonic, brief, generalized) or complex (focal onset, >15 min, or recurrence within 24 h).

In low‑resource settings, the leading causes are viral infections (cough, cold, gastroenteritis), malaria, and bacterial meningitis. Other contributors include HIV, sickle cell crises, and parasitic infections.

t.b: CSF shows neutrophils, high protein, low glucose

sections.p: Children sit up, stiffen, then fall. Eyes roll, lips may cyanose, and the seizure lasts a few minutes. Post‑ictal confusion is brief.
Only essential tests are performed when resources allow. In many settings, a full septic work‑up is not feasible, so clinical judgment guides management.
Severe or prolonged seizures, focal deficits, or signs of meningitis (neck stiffness, photophobia) require urgent care. Recurrent seizures may herald epilepsy.

sections.p: Treat the underlying infection, control fever, and provide supportive care. Benzodiazepines are first‑line for acute seizures; avoid antiepileptics unless seizures recur.

t.b: Coverage for common pathogens (e.g., ceftriaxone for meningitis)

sections.p: Reassure parents, advise on fever control, and counsel on when to seek help. No routine prophylaxis is recommended.
Seizures due to meningitis, encephalitis, hypoglycaemia, or metabolic derangements can mimic febrile convulsions.
A normal CBC may miss early bacterial infection; a negative malaria test does not exclude parasitaemia in high‑endemic areas.
